clue.text: Fowles's sorcerer found in short-story mag (US style)

indicators.note: found in says the letters sit inside the words that follow, running across the bracket

explanation.surface: A wizard figure turns up in a short story printed by an American magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' points inside 'mag (US style)': read the letters straight through, ignoring the bracket. John Fowles's novel The Magus centres on the sorcerer-like Conchis.
explanation.definitionFit: The Magus is the title of John Fowles's novel, and a magus is a magician or wizard.

clue.text: Lively bright burner, being undisciplined, or emoting

indicators.note: undisciplined letters run wild and out of order, so the words or emoting are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fiery, unruly performer emotes wildly on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Penelope Lively's Booker-winning Moon Tiger is named after a slow-burning mosquito coil; 'bright burner' also nods to Blake's tiger burning bright, and 'Lively' is the author, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope Lively wrote the novel Moon Tiger, whose title is a smouldering insect-repellent coil, a burner.

clue.text: His master would have his bond

definitions.text: His master would have his bond

parts.words: His master would have his bond
parts.note: Shylock in The Merchant of Venice insists 'I'll have my bond'; the clue describes the clown who served him

explanation.definitionFit: Launcelot is the servant of Shylock, the moneylender who demands his bond in The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: Where spicy breezes blow soft, these days, suggests Reginald Heber

definitions.text: Where spicy breezes blow soft, these days, suggests Reginald Heber

parts.words: Where spicy breezes blow soft, these days, suggests Reginald Heber
parts.note: Heber's hymn From Greenland's Icy Mountains has spicy breezes blowing soft o'er Ceylon's isle; the island's modern name is wanted

explanation.definitionFit: Heber's hymn names Ceylon, the island now called by its present-day name since 1972.

clue.text: Rose Macaulay's contribution to gamesmanship?

parts.note: Rose Macaulay wrote a satirical novel with this title; gamesmanship is the coinage of Stephen Potter, so his doctrine would be named the same way

explanation.definitionFit: Macaulay's 1920 satirical novel bears this title, and the word would also suit the creed of Stephen Potter, author of Gamesmanship.

clue.text: Theatre piece by Beckett

parts.note: Samuel Beckett wrote a short drama whose title is simply the generic word for a stage work

explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's 1963 one-act drama is titled with the ordinary word for any stage drama.

clue.text: Firm in hackneyed employment for Madame Defarge, say

indicators.note: in places the firm inside the word for hackneyed

parts.note: hackneyed means trite, worn out
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
employment means use

explanation.surface: A firm finds a tired old job for a famous villainess of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Madame Defarge in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities knits beside the guillotine, the classic knitting woman of the French Revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame Defarge is the best-known example of the women who knitted while watching executions during the Terror.

clue.text: Striking effects of ruined castle

indicators.note: a ruined building has its stones tumbled, so the letters of castle fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A ruined castle makes a dramatic sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived word means brilliant displays or dazzling successes, things that make a striking show.

clue.text: One member travelling, and getting better

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
MP is a Member of Parliament
travelling means roving, wandering about

explanation.surface: A parliamentarian on his travels is recovering his health.
explanation.definitionFit: Improving describes a patient or situation on the mend, becoming better.

clue.text: J.C. Harris character in Wyoming omnibus

indicators.note: in tells us the name lies within the words Wyoming omnibus, across their join

explanation.surface: A figure from the Uncle Remus stories rides a bus across Wyoming.
explanation.walkthrough: Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus, wrote a story with a character called Mingo.
explanation.definitionFit: Joel Chandler Harris used this name for a character in his stories of the American South.

clue.text: Essential points of arrangement

parts.note: a musical arrangement's essential parts are those marked as indispensable, the Italian plural for obligatory instrumental parts

explanation.definitionFit: In music, an obbligato is an instrumental part that must not be left out of the arrangement; the Italian plural is used.

clue.text: Bloomer made by gentleman thief

explanation.surface: A botanical blunder perpetrated by a suave burglar.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is a flowering plant, here the tall flower spike of the pea family; Arsène is the gentleman burglar of Maurice Leblanc's stories.

clue.text: Cartographer of Love

parts.note: Dylan wrote the collection The Map of Love, so he is its mapmaker

explanation.definitionFit: Dylan, the Welsh poet, published The Map of Love in 1939, making him its mapmaker.

clue.text: Conrad masterwork confusing to morons

indicators.note: confusing jumbles the words to morons into a different sequence

explanation.surface: A great novel by Conrad that baffles the dim-witted.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Conrad's 1904 novel set in the fictional republic of Costaguana is often reckoned his greatest work.

clue.text: Borrow character from Ambrose Smith

parts.note: George Borrow modelled the Romany figure in Lavengro on the real gypsy Ambrose Smith

explanation.definitionFit: Jasper, the Romany friend in George Borrow's Lavengro, was based on the real gypsy Ambrose Smith.

clue.text: Post with certain perks at Wragby Hall

definitions.text: Post with certain perks at Wragby Hall

parts.words: Post with certain perks at Wragby Hall
parts.note: Wragby Hall is Clifford Chatterley's estate, where Mellors holds the job of looking after the pheasants, and enjoys Lady Chatterley

explanation.definitionFit: Mellors, Lady Chatterley's lover, is employed at Wragby Hall to rear and guard game birds.

clue.text: Upset main Latin character from Nicholas Nickleby

indicators.note: upset tips the words main Latin over so their letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: A Dickens figure upset by the principal Latin lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Mantalini is the foppish husband of the dressmaker Madame Mantalini in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Mantalini, the extravagant dandy married to a dressmaker, appears in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.

clue.text: De la Mare's Laetitia knew the rhyme about the hickory one

definitions.text: De la Mare's Laetitia knew the rhyme about the hickory one

parts.words: De la Mare's Laetitia knew the rhyme about the hickory one
parts.note: the nursery rhyme goes 'hang your clothes on a hickory' branch 'but don't go near the water'; Walter de la Mare's poem about Laetitia alludes to it

explanation.definitionFit: A limb is a tree branch, as in the rhyme's hickory branch where the clothes are hung.

clue.text: Plagiarizers of Mary Norton?

parts.note: Mary Norton wrote about tiny people who take things from the humans' house; plagiarists likewise take what is not theirs

explanation.definitionFit: Plagiarists take others' words, and Mary Norton's little people live by taking small household items.

clue.text: Early viticulturist and good-time Charlie

parts.note: the Greek god of wine taught mankind to grow vines and presided over revelry

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of wine and revelry was credited with first cultivating the vine.

clue.text: Associated with the book by Browning

definitions.text: Associated with the book by Browning

parts.words: Associated with the book by Browning
parts.note: Robert Browning wrote the long poem The ___ and the Book, so the missing title word sits alongside the book

explanation.definitionFit: Browning's long poem is The Ring and the Book, so the band of gold is paired with the book.

clue.text: Firearms hang around a Zane Grey character?

parts.note: firearms means guns
to hang around is to linger

explanation.surface: Weapons dangle idly near a hero of Zane Grey's westerns.
explanation.definitionFit: Zane Grey wrote westerns full of quick-draw gunfighters; the question mark admits this is a type, not a named figure.

clue.text: "-, peel me a grape." (Mae West)

parts.note: in the film I'm No Angel Mae West orders her maid, addressed by name, to peel her a grape

explanation.definitionFit: Mae West's famous line in I'm No Angel is addressed to her maid, played by Gertrude Howard.

clue.text: Poet and general who proved elusive

parts.note: William Blake is the poet
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals, a general

explanation.surface: A poet and a soldier who could never be caught.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Percy Blakeney is the Scarlet Pimpernel, famous for eluding the French: 'They seek him here, they seek him there.'
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Percy, the Scarlet Pimpernel, is the hero whom the revolutionaries could never catch.

clue.text: We are seen in good French novelist ()

indicators.note: are seen in says the first word appears inside the French for good

parts.note: the French word for good is bon
taken as written

explanation.surface: We are found in a fine French novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The empty brackets at the end are a stray from the printing. Elizabeth Bowen was the Anglo-Irish novelist of The Heat of the Day.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Bowen was an Anglo-Irish author of novels such as The Death of the Heart.

clue.text: Private character of Linklater

parts.note: Eric Linklater wrote the novel Private ___, about an Italian soldier, so 'Private' is his rank

explanation.definitionFit: Eric Linklater's novel Private Angelo follows a reluctant Italian soldier through the Second World War.

clue.text: Oration from English box

parts.note: a loge is a box in a theatre

explanation.surface: A speech delivered from an English theatre box.
explanation.definitionFit: An eloge is a formal speech of praise, especially a funeral eulogy.

clue.text: Eppie (as in Civil Service)

indicators.note: in places the little word as inside the abbreviation for Civil Service

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl's name, as used in the Civil Service.
explanation.walkthrough: In George Eliot's Silas Marner, Eppie is the natural daughter of Godfrey Cass, raised by Silas.
explanation.definitionFit: Eppie in Silas Marner is by birth the daughter of Godfrey, of the squire's family, so this is her blood surname.

clue.text: Vile sound of cheap opera composer

indicators.note: sound of means the word is said aloud, in the German way the composer's name is spoken

parts.note: vile is the word heard, matching the German pronunciation of the surname

explanation.surface: An awful noise from a composer of low-budget opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Kurt Weill wrote The Threepenny Opera, hence 'cheap opera'; in German his name is pronounced like 'vile'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kurt Weill composed The Threepenny Opera, whose title makes it a cheap opera.

clue.text: Premier student of Homer

explanation.surface: A prime minister who studied Homer.
explanation.definitionFit: W. E. Gladstone was four times British Prime Minister and also wrote scholarly studies of the Iliad and Odyssey.

clue.text: Proto-soap of Thomas Berger?

parts.note: Thomas Berger's 1980 novel shares its title, American spelling, with the later Australian television soap

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Berger's 1980 novel bears the title later used, British-spelt, by the Australian TV soap about a suburban street.

clue.text: ".. fondly here admire Fair seeming, and feed on vain delight" (Spenser)

definitions.text: ".. fondly here admire Fair seeming, and feed on vain delight" (Spenser)

parts.words: ".. fondly here admire Fair seeming, and feed on vain delight" (Spenser)
parts.note: the gap in Spenser's line is an old spelling of a verb meaning displays

explanation.definitionFit: The archaic spelling of 'shows', meaning displays, completes Spenser's line about admiring fair appearances.
